summary: Davis may be the only city in America where bikes outnumber cars on certain roads — it earned designation as the country's first platinum-level bicycle-friendly city from the League of American Bicyclists, and the flat Sacramento Valley floor makes that infrastructure genuinely practical rather than aspirational. The terrain is dead-level agricultural plain, which means open-sky horizons in every direction, spectacular sunsets behind the Coast Range to the west, and summer highs that routinely push well above the 76°F annual average — July and August days frequently top 100°F, though nearly 9.6 hours of daily sunshine and negligible humidity keep mornings and evenings comfortable. UC Davis, the city's dominant employer and economic engine, anchors a compact 10-square-mile footprint at a walkable 6,571 people per square mile; the university and its medical system mean that switching jobs without leaving town is realistic mainly within education, research, and healthcare. The tradeoff is stark: a median home price of $829,000 against a median household income of $87,421 yields a price-to-income ratio above 9.5, and a 25.1% poverty rate — largely reflective of the enormous graduate-student population — coexists with some of the highest educational attainment in the state (75.1% holding a bachelor's degree or higher). A well-connected greenbelt system threads through the city, linking parks and bike paths so that evening walks rarely require a car. Davis is essentially a research university that grew a town around it, and the housing math reflects that tension between a small-city footprint and big-city price expectations.
